How the AI works, step by step
Isolates the fruit on a gray background
Segments the fruit and the lesions
Computes the area percentage and the class

The camera works in maximum-quality mode, at the sensor\'s highest 4:3 resolution and with JPEG quality 95. Before shooting, it focuses and adjusts exposure at the tapped point or the center of the frame. The preview shows exactly what ends up in the photo.

Every image, whether from the camera or the gallery, gets the same treatment: the rotation stored in the EXIF data is corrected and the longest side is limited to 2048 px, the value used to prepare the training photos.

To enter each network, the image is scaled while keeping its proportions and is completed with gray bands (114, 114, 114) to form a square. This technique is called letterboxing. Pixels are converted to RGB in the 0 to 1 range.

A single-class YOLO26n-seg network whose task is to find the fruit, so a 480 px input is enough. The most confident detection is used. If none reaches 0.25, the app asks you to retake the photo instead of giving a result.

The fruit box is cropped with a 10% margin. Pixels outside the mask, expanded by 0.4% to keep the edge, are replaced with gray (128, 128, 128). This stops Model B from relying on the background, which almost predicts the class in the dataset.
This crop sets the available detail. If the fruit covers less than 640 px in the photo, it is enlarged without gaining real information and the app shows a notice asking you to move closer.
A four-class YOLO26n-seg network: the fruit and three lesions. It works on the crop at 640 px and produces one mask for each detection with a confidence of at least 0.25.
Each detection has a box, a confidence, a class and 32 coefficients. The network also outputs 32 prototypes, which are base images. The mask combines both:

The result is enlarged with bilinear interpolation to the input size, kept only inside the box, binarized with a 0.5 threshold, and stripped of the letterbox bands. The models are end-to-end, so they do not need non-maximum suppression (NMS).

Each lesion uses the same formula with its own mask. The image is considered healthy if total severity is below 0.5%; otherwise it takes the name of the lesion with the largest area. The overall classification uses these ranges:
The 1 to 10 scale for each damage uses these limits, as a percentage of area:
The classification ranges and the 1 to 10 scale are initial values and must be calibrated with agronomists.
Per-image classification on the test split: 142 photos of fruits not used for training. The 95% confidence interval for accuracy runs from 73% to 86%.
Confirm a \"healthy\" result by eye: 44% of the photos the model called healthy had lesions. It also recognized only 52% of the fruits with oil spot.

These figures come from the dataset photos; performance may differ on field photos. Area metrics are not reported because the lesion masks were trained on automatic pseudo-labels (PatchCore + SAM) that depend on expert review. Treat severity as an approximate estimate.

The models were exported to ONNX and quantized to int8, making them about 3.4 times smaller. ONNX Runtime runs them on the CPU with 4 threads. They load during the first analysis and stay ready for the next ones.
Check against PyTorch (30 images): mean IoU and same main detection
Each analysis stores its inference times, photo resolution and crop size under \"Technical details\" in the result.
Photos of purple passion fruit from four classes were used: healthy, scab, anthracnose and oil spot. The split was made per fruit, so the same fruit never appears in two splits.
The lesion masks come from automatic pseudo-labels generated with PatchCore and SAM, not from manual annotation.
By default the analysis runs on the phone: the photo does not leave the device and no internet is needed. The history is also stored only on the phone.
If you turn off local inference in Settings, the photo is sent to an optional remote server that uses a different analysis process (YOLO11 and Chan-Vese) from the one described here.
Demo mode shows simulated data and does not analyze the photo. Do not use its values to make decisions.
The percentage refers to the side visible in the photo, not the whole fruit surface.
Only three lesions on purple passion fruit are recognized. Other damage or other fruits are not identified correctly.
The result is an approximate aid and does not replace an agronomist\'s diagnosis.
Local analysis does not compute the area in cm² because the photo has no scale reference.
A good result starts before you open the camera.
Photograph one fruit at a time.
Remove dust or moisture without rubbing the skin.
Prefer soft natural light and avoid direct sun and reflections.
Move closer until the fruit almost fills the frame.
What you see on screen is what ends up in the photo.
The more pixels the fruit covers, the easier it is to distinguish small lesions.
A blurry photo erases the lesions the model needs to see.
Tap the fruit on the screen: a yellow ring will appear.
If you are too close, the camera cannot focus. Move back a few centimeters.
Hold the phone still: the app focuses again before shooting, which can take up to 2 seconds.
Press the round button or open your gallery.
Use the flash only in low light, because it can cause reflections on the skin.
From the gallery, choose original photos, not images forwarded through messaging apps, which arrive compressed.
To check the whole fruit, photograph each side separately.
Everything happens on your phone, with no internet.
Model A finds the fruit and removes the background.
Model B looks for scab, anthracnose and oil spot.
If it does not find a fruit, it will ask you to take another photo.
You will see the area percentage of each lesion and an overall classification.
In the image, red marks scab, purple anthracnose and orange oil spot.
If the result is \"healthy\", confirm it by eye: the model can miss some lesions.
If a low-detail notice appears, retake the photo from closer.
Keep your analyses and share them with your team.
Save the analysis to see it later in your previous reports.
Generate the PDF sheet or download the original and processed images.
From the history you can also export all your analyses to CSV.

Block in excellent phytosanitary condition. Keep up sucker removal, aeration pruning and weekly monitoring to maintain the export rating.
Early damage spots identified (< 5%). Carry out selective sanitary pruning of affected leaves and tendrils. Apply preventive copper-based disinfectants or biofungicides.
Moderate severity (5-20%). Sorting for the domestic market or processed pulp is suggested. Assess relative humidity and apply a rotation of fungicides with curative action.
Fruit with severe damage (> 20%). Phytosanitary discard for export. Remove diseased fruit from the plantation to avoid spreading inoculum and consult an agronomist immediately.
